name: Anammelek
title: The Idol of the Sepharvites
summary: Anammelek was one of the idols that the Sepharvites — the people from Sepharvaim — brought with them to Samaria after the Assyrian king deported them there following the fall of the Northern Kingdom (722 B.C.). In 2 Kings 17:31, it is described how the Sepharvites sacrificed their own children by burning them in fire as an offering to Anammelek and the related idol Adrammelek. This gruesome practice serves in the biblical account as a striking example of the pagan idolatry that filled the religious void after Israel’s exile. Etymologically, the name has been linked to the Akkadian sky god Anu ('Anu is king'), but the interpretation remains uncertain. The entire context of 2 Kings 17 emphasizes that turning away from the Lord led to judgment and exile, and that the syncretistic religious practices that arose in Samaria stood in deep opposition to covenant faithfulness toward Israel’s God.

keyEvents.title: Assyrian Relocation to Samaria
keyEvents.description: After the Assyrian king conquered the northern kingdom of Israel, people from several nations, including Sepharvaim, were settled in the cities of Samaria. These peoples brought their own gods and idols with them.

keyEvents.title: Child Sacrifice by the Sepharvites to Anammelek and Adrammelek
keyEvents.description: The people of Sepharvaim burned their children in fire as an offering to the idols Adrammelek and Anammelek. This abominable practice stood in sharp contrast to the Lord's commands and illustrates the depth of pagan idolatry that took place in Samaria.

keyEvents.title: Syncretistic Religious Practice in Samaria
keyEvents.description: The foreign peoples in Samaria worshiped both the Lord and their own gods, leading to a religious mixture that was strongly condemned in the biblical account as an expression of apostasy and covenant breaking.

keyEvents.title: The Biblical Context: Israel's Sin and Judgment
keyEvents.description: The chapter in 2 Kings explains that Israel's fall and the subsequent idolatry in the land were consequences of the people's persistent sin and turning away from the Lord. This theological framework shows why foreign peoples and their idols, including Anammelek, ended up in Samaria.

The worship of Anammelek involved child sacrifice, where children were burned in fire as an offering to this god. Anammelek is mentioned together with the idol Adrammelek in 2 Kings, and their worship serves as an example of the idolatry that the biblical author condemns as the cause of Israel's fall.

footnotes.text: The name Anammelech may possibly be derived from the Akkadian Anu-malik, meaning 'Anu is king,' linking the deity to the Mesopotamian sky god Anu. However, some scholars have proposed alternative etymologies, including a connection to the Elamite goddess Anahita or a distortion of another Semitic divine name.

Sepharvaim is often identified with the ancient city of Sippar in Mesopotamia, which was an important cultic center for the sun god Shamash. Other scholars suggest an identification with Shabarain mentioned in Assyrian inscriptions, or with two cities (the dual form in Hebrew suggesting 'the two Sippars').

The Assyrian practice of deporting and resettling conquered peoples is well documented in Assyrian source texts, such as the annals of Sargon II, and in reliefs from Assyrian palaces. This policy was used systematically to break down national cohesion and prevent uprisings in conquered territories.

Child sacrifice to gods like Adrammelech and Anammelech was a practice consistently condemned in biblical material. Similar condemnation is found in connection with Molech worship (Lev 18:21; 20:2–5), and the prophets repeatedly warned against this custom (Jer 7:31; 19:5; Ezek 16:20–21).

The religious syncretism described in 2 Kings 17—where the new inhabitants worshiped both the Lord and their own gods—is regarded by many scholars as part of the background for the development of Samaritan religion and the long-standing conflict between Jews and Samaritans in later periods.

It is worth noting that Anammelech is mentioned only once in the entire Bible (2 Kings 17:31). Everything we know about this deity from biblical sources is limited to this single verse, and there are very few extrabiblical sources that can shed further light on the cult. This makes Anammelech one of the most obscure divine names in the Old Testament.
